smt-2018-team-01.title: Chord of a parabola
smt-2018-team-01.body:
The chord through $(p,p^2)$ and $(q,q^2)$ has slope $\frac{q^2-p^2}{q-p}=p+q$, so its equation is $y-p^2=(p+q)(x-p)$, i.e. $y=(p+q)x-pq$. Its $y$-intercept is $-pq=-(-29)(51)=1479$.

**Answer: 1479**

smt-2018-team-02.title: Surface area grows linearly
smt-2018-team-02.body:
Joining $n$ prisms end to end adds $2(x+y)z$ of lateral area per extra prism, so the surface area is linear in $n$: $S(n)=S(1)+(n-1)\Delta$. From $S(11)=3S(1)$ we get $10\Delta=2S(1)$. For $S(n)=9S(1)$ we need $(n-1)\Delta=8S(1)$, i.e. $n-1=8\cdot\frac{10}{2}=40$, so $n=41$.

**Answer: 41**

smt-2018-team-02.title: Algebra
smt-2018-team-02.body:
With the end faces $x\times y$ and length $z$, $S(n)=2xy+2(x+y)nz$. Setting $S(11)=3S(1)$: $2xy+22(x+y)z=6xy+6(x+y)z$, so $16(x+y)z=4xy$, i.e. $xy=4(x+y)z$. For $S(n)=9S(1)$: $2xy+2(x+y)nz=18xy+18(x+y)z$ so $(x+y)z(2n-18)=16xy=64(x+y)z$, giving $n=41$.

**Answer: 41**

smt-2018-team-03.title: Half of the rectangle
smt-2018-team-03.body:
The hypotenuse $10x+9y=180$ contains lattice points $(0,20),(9,10),(18,0)$: $3$ points. The $21\times19$ lattice rectangle has $399$ points; the diagonal's $3$ points are counted in both triangles, so the triangle has $\frac{399+3}{2}=201$ points.

**Answer: 201**

smt-2018-team-03.title: Pick's theorem
smt-2018-team-03.body:
Area $=180$, boundary points $=20+18+\gcd(18,20)=40$. Interior points $I=A-\frac B2+1=180-20+1=161$. Total $=161+40=201$.

**Answer: 201**

smt-2018-team-04.title: Parity
smt-2018-team-04.body:
If $n$ were odd, all divisors would be odd and $a_3^3-a_2^3$ would be even, a contradiction. So $n$ is even and $a_2=2$. Then $n=a_3^3-8$ must be even, so $a_3$ is even, $a_3=2k$. Then $k\mid n$ with $k<a_3$, so $k\in\{1,2\}$. $k=1$ gives $a_3=2=a_2$, impossible, so $k=2$ and $a_3=4$. Then $n=64-8=56$, whose divisors are $1,2,4,7,8,\ldots$ - consistent.

**Answer: 56**

smt-2018-team-05.title: Coprime lattice points
smt-2018-team-05.body:
$ax_0+by_0=1$ has integer solutions $(a,b)$ exactly when $\gcd(x_0,y_0)=1$. So count lattice points on $(x-2)^2+(y+3)^2=25$ with coprime coordinates. The $12$ lattice points are $(-3,-3),(-2,-6),(-2,0),(-1,-7),(-1,1),(2,-8),(2,2),(5,-7),(5,1),(6,-6),(6,0),(7,-3)$ (offsets $(\pm5,0),(0,\pm5),(\pm3,\pm4),(\pm4,\pm3)$). The coprime ones are $(-1,-7),(-1,1),(5,-7),(5,1),(7,-3)$: $5$ points.

**Answer: 5**

smt-2018-team-06.title: Thales
smt-2018-team-06.body:
A triangle inscribed in a circle is right iff two vertices are diametrically opposite. There are $1009$ diameters and $2016$ choices of the third vertex, so $1009\cdot2016$ right triangles out of $\binom{2018}{3}=\frac{2018\cdot2017\cdot2016}{6}$. The probability is $\frac{1009\cdot2016\cdot6}{2018\cdot2017\cdot2016}=\frac{3}{2017}$.

**Answer: $\frac3{2017}$**

smt-2018-team-07.title: Pigeonhole plus construction
smt-2018-team-07.body:
The $x$-coordinates of the $5$ points lie in $[-1,1]$; sorted, the $4$ gaps sum to at most $2$, so $m_x\le\frac12$, and likewise $m_y,m_z\le\frac12$. So $m_x+m_y+m_z\le\frac32$. Equality needs every coordinate to be in $\{-1,-\frac12,0,\frac12,1\}$, each value used once per axis. The points $(-1,\frac12,0),(-\frac12,1,-1),(0,-1,-\frac12),(\frac12,0,1),(1,-\frac12,\frac12)$ achieve this, and each lies on the surface because it has a coordinate of absolute value $1$.

**Answer: $\frac32$**

smt-2018-team-08.title: AM-GM
smt-2018-team-08.body:
Let the total dots on $A$ be $a$ and on $B$ be $b$, $a+b=36$. By independence the expected product is $\left(\frac a6\right)^2\cdot\frac b6=\frac{a^2b}{216}$. By AM-GM, $\frac a2\cdot\frac a2\cdot b\le\left(\frac{a+b}{3}\right)^3=12^3$, with equality at $\frac a2=b$, i.e. $a=24$, $b=12$ (possible: put $4$ dots on each face of $A$ and $2$ on each face of $B$). Then $a^2b=24^2\cdot12=6912$ and the expected product is $\frac{6912}{216}=32$.

**Answer: 32**

smt-2018-team-09.title: Ptolemy
smt-2018-team-09.body:
$\angle ABF=\angle CBE$ gives $\angle EBF=\angle CBA=90^\circ$, so $\triangle EBF$ is a right isosceles triangle with $EF=2\sqrt5\cdot\sqrt2=2\sqrt{10}$. Since $AEBF$ is cyclic, $\angle EAF=180^\circ-90^\circ=90^\circ$, so $AF=\sqrt{EF^2-AE^2}=\sqrt{40-36}=2$. Ptolemy on $AEBF$ (diagonals $AB$ and $EF$): $AB\cdot EF=AE\cdot BF+AF\cdot BE=6\cdot2\sqrt5+2\cdot2\sqrt5=16\sqrt5$. So $AB=\frac{16\sqrt5}{2\sqrt{10}}=4\sqrt2$ and the area is $32$.

**Answer: 32**

smt-2018-team-10.title: Remove the ordering
smt-2018-team-10.body:
Put $a=w,\ b=x-w,\ c=y-x,\ d=z-y\ge0$. Then $5w+3x+y+z=10a+5b+2c+d$, so we count nonnegative solutions of $10a+5b+2c+d=100$. For each $(a,b,c)$ with $10a+5b+2c\le100$ the value of $d$ is determined. Let $j=2a+b$ ($0\le j\le20$), which has $\lfloor j/2\rfloor+1$ representations, and then $c$ takes $\left\lfloor\frac{100-5j}{2}\right\rfloor+1$ values. The total is $\sum_{j=0}^{20}\left(\lfloor\tfrac j2\rfloor+1\right)\left(\lfloor\tfrac{100-5j}2\rfloor+1\right)=2156$ (evaluated and confirmed by computer; the official solution gets $286+1540+330=2156$ by casework on the $10$'s).

**Answer: 2156**

smt-2018-team-11.title: Euler product
smt-2018-team-11.body:
Only $k=2^m3^n$ contribute, and $\frac{f(k)}{k}=\frac m{2^m}\cdot\frac n{3^n}$. So the sum factors: $\left(1+\sum_{m\ge1}\frac m{2^m}\right)\left(1+\sum_{n\ge1}\frac n{3^n}\right)$. Using $\sum_{m\ge1}mx^m=\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}$: $\sum\frac m{2^m}=2$ and $\sum\frac n{3^n}=\frac{1/3}{4/9}=\frac34$. The product is $3\cdot\frac74=\frac{21}{4}$.

**Answer: $\frac{21}4$**

smt-2018-team-13.title: Key fact: $PQ=DE+DF$
smt-2018-team-13.body:
$DEF$ is the orthic triangle of $ABC$, and $A,B,C$ are the excenters of $DEF$ opposite $D,E,F$. Let $\omega_1$ be the excircle centered at $B$ and $\omega_2$ the excircle centered at $C$; both are tangent to the three lines $DE,DF,EF$. Since $BP\perp EF$ and $CQ\perp EF$, $P$ and $Q$ are the tangency points on $EF$, so $PQ$ is a common external tangent of $\omega_1,\omega_2$, while lines $DE$ and $DF$ are common internal tangents.

Let the other external tangent be $P'Q'$, and let $DF$ touch $\omega_1$ at $X$ and $\omega_2$ at $Y$; let $DF$ meet $P'Q'$ at $E'$. Equal tangent lengths give $FP=FX$, $FQ=FY$, $E'P'=E'X$, $E'Q'=E'Y$, and $PQ=P'Q'$ by symmetry, so
$2PQ=(FP+FQ)+(E'P'+E'Q')=(FX+E'X)+(FY+E'Y)=2E'F$, i.e. $PQ=E'F$. Reflecting across $BC$ swaps $E$ and $E'$ and fixes $D$, so $DE'=DE$ and $E'F=DE'+DF=DE+DF$. Thus $PQ=DE+DF$ (also confirmed numerically on a sample triangle).

Then $DE+(DE-4)=2018$, so $DE=1011$.

**Answer: 1011**

smt-2018-team-14.title: Independence
smt-2018-team-14.body:
Area $=\frac12\,OA\cdot OB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $OA$ and $OB$. $OA$, $OB$, $\theta$ are independent. The density of the distance from $O$ is $2r$ on $[0,1]$, so $E[OA]=\int_0^12r^2dr=\frac23$. The angle is uniform, so $E[\sin\theta]=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta=\frac2\pi$ (using the unsigned angle in $[0,\pi]$). Hence $E=\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac2\pi=\frac{4}{9\pi}$.

**Answer: $\frac{4}{9\pi}$**

smt-2018-team-15.title: Factor and AM-GM
smt-2018-team-15.body:
Divide the first equation by $bc$ and add $1$: $\frac{25a}{c}+\frac{25a}{b}+\frac bc+1=15$, which factors as $(25a+b)\left(\frac1b+\frac1c\right)=15$. In the same way (dividing by $cd$, $da$, $ab$ and adding $9$, $25$, $20$ respectively):
$(4b+9c)\left(\frac1c+\frac1d\right)=40,\quad(9c+25d)\left(\frac1d+\frac1a\right)=120,\quad(5d+20a)\left(\frac1a+\frac1b\right)=36.$

Multiply all four and regroup by pairs of variables:
$\left(26+25\frac ab+\frac ba\right)\left(13+4\frac bc+9\frac cb\right)\left(34+9\frac cd+25\frac dc\right)\left(25+5\frac da+20\frac ad\right)=15\cdot40\cdot120\cdot36.$
By AM-GM, $25\frac ab+\frac ba\ge10$, $4\frac bc+9\frac cb\ge12$, $9\frac cd+25\frac dc\ge30$, $5\frac da+20\frac ad\ge20$, so the left side is at least $36\cdot25\cdot64\cdot45=15\cdot40\cdot120\cdot36$. Equality holds, so every AM-GM is an equality: $25\frac ab=\frac ba$, $4\frac bc=9\frac cb$, $9\frac cd=25\frac dc$, $5\frac da=20\frac ad$. Hence $\frac ab=\frac15,\ \frac bc=\frac32,\ \frac cd=\frac53,\ \frac da=2$ and the requested sum is $\frac15+\frac32+\frac53+2=\frac{161}{30}$. (A solution exists: $(a,b,c,d)=(3,15,10,6)$.)

**Answer: $\frac{161}{30}$**

smt-2018-team-p1.title: Squares modulo 7
smt-2018-team-p1.body: The squares mod $7$ are $0,1,2,4$. If $7\mid a^2+b^2+1$ then $a^2+b^2\equiv6\pmod7$. Checking sums of two squares from $\{0,1,2,4\}$: $0+0,0+1,0+2,0+4,1+1,1+2,1+4,2+2,2+4,4+4\equiv0,1,2,4,2,3,5,4,6,1$. Only $2+4\equiv6$ works, so (up to swapping) $a^2\equiv2$ and $b^2\equiv4\pmod7$. Then $a\equiv\pm3$ and $b\equiv\pm2\pmod7$. The possible values of $a+b\pmod 7$ are $\pm5,\pm1$, i.e. $\{5,2,1,6\}$ - never $0$. So $7\nmid a+b$. $\blacksquare$

smt-2018-team-p1.title: Direct contradiction
smt-2018-team-p1.body: Suppose $7\mid a+b$, so $b\equiv-a\pmod7$ and $b^2\equiv a^2$. Then $0\equiv a^2+b^2+1\equiv2a^2+1$, so $2a^2\equiv-1\equiv6$ and $a^2\equiv3\pmod7$. But $3$ is not a square mod $7$ (the squares are $0,1,2,4$), a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

smt-2018-team-p2.title: Recurrence on the occupancy
smt-2018-team-p2.body:
Let $t_k\in\{0,1\}$ indicate a token at $k$, with $t_0=t_{n+1}=0$. A position is static iff for all $1\le k\le n$: $t_k=1$ exactly when exactly one of $t_{k-1},t_{k+1}$ is $1$, i.e. $t_k\equiv t_{k-1}+t_{k+1}\pmod2$, i.e. $t_{k+1}\equiv t_k+t_{k-1}\pmod2$.

So the whole position is determined by $t_1=x$: $t_0=0,\ t_1=x,\ t_2=x,\ t_3=0,\ t_4=x,\ t_5=x,\ t_6=0,\ldots$, i.e. $t_k=x$ if $3\nmid k$ and $t_k=0$ if $3\mid k$. The trivial position is $x=0$. For $x=1$ the position is non-trivial, and the boundary condition $t_{n+1}=0$ holds iff $3\mid n+1$, i.e. $n\equiv2\pmod3$.

Hence: if $n\not\equiv2\pmod3$ there is no non-trivial static position; if $n\equiv2\pmod3$ there is exactly one, with tokens on precisely the positions $k$ not divisible by $3$ (for example $n=5$: tokens at $1,2,4,5$, written XX_XX). $\blacksquare$

smt-2018-team-p3.title: Reduce to integer differences
smt-2018-team-p3.body:
We have $\begin{pmatrix}a-c\\b-d\end{pmatrix}=x\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}+y\begin{pmatrix}5\\3\end{pmatrix}$. Since $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}=3\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}5\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}=2\begin{pmatrix}5\\3\end{pmatrix}-5\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$, every integer vector $\begin{pmatrix}m\\n\end{pmatrix}$ is of the form $x(2,1)+y(5,3)$ with integers $x,y$. So it suffices to find two distinct points of $A$ whose difference is an integer vector.

Cut the plane into the unit squares $[i,i+1)\times[j,j+1)$ and translate each piece $A\cap$(square) by an integer vector into $[0,1)^2$. Translations by integer vectors preserve area, so the images have total area equal to $\text{area}(A)>1$, while they all lie in a region of area $1$. Hence two pieces overlap: some point $P\in[0,1)^2$ is the image of two distinct points $(a,b)\ne(c,d)$ of $A$ (in different squares). They differ by the difference of the two integer translations, an integer vector. $\blacksquare$

smt-2018-team-p4.title: Binet formula
smt-2018-team-p4.body:
With the standard Fibonacci numbers $f_0=0,f_1=1$ we have $F_k=f_{k+1}=\frac{\varphi^{k+1}-\psi^{k+1}}{\sqrt5}$, where $\varphi,\psi$ are the roots of $t^2=t+1$, $\varphi\psi=-1$. Put $\alpha=\varphi^n$, $\beta=\psi^n$. Then $F_{nk}=u\alpha^k-v\beta^k$ for constants $u=\frac{\varphi}{\sqrt5},\ v=\frac{\psi}{\sqrt5}$. Any sequence of the form $p\alpha^k+q\beta^k$ satisfies $s_{k+1}=(\alpha+\beta)s_k-\alpha\beta\,s_{k-1}$, because $\alpha,\beta$ are the roots of $t^2-(\alpha+\beta)t+\alpha\beta$. So $b=\alpha+\beta$ and $c=-\alpha\beta=-(\varphi\psi)^n=-(-1)^n$ work.

The constants are unique: the equations for $k=1,2$ are $F_{2n}=bF_n+cF_0$ and $F_{3n}=bF_{2n}+cF_n$, a linear system in $(b,c)$ with determinant $F_n^2-F_0F_{2n}=f_{n+1}^2-f_{2n+1}=-f_n^2\ne0$ (using $f_{2n+1}=f_{n+1}^2+f_n^2$). Therefore the given $b_n,c_n$ are these values and $|c_n|=|-(-1)^n|=1$. $\blacksquare$

smt-2018-team-p5.title: Reduce to quadratics, then triangle inequality
smt-2018-team-p5.body:
Write $X=AB+BC+CD+DA$, $Y=AC+BD$, $Z=Y+AB+CD$.

**Step 1.** Since $AB+CD>2>1$, $(AB+CD)^3>(AB+CD)^2$. Since $|AC-BC|<1$ and $|BD-AD|<1$,
$|AC^3-BC^3|=|AC-BC|(AC^2+BC^2+AC\cdot BC)<AC^2+BC^2+AC\cdot BC$ and $|BD^3-AD^3|<BD^2+AD^2+BD\cdot AD$.
Hence $2|AC^3-BC^3|+2|BD^3-AD^3|<S'':=2(AC^2+BC^2+AD^2+BD^2)+2(AC\cdot BC+BD\cdot AD)\le2(AC^2+BC^2+AD^2+BD^2)+2(AC+BD)(BC+AD)$. So the right side of the claimed inequality is less than $S''-(AB+CD)^2$, and it suffices to show
$$(X+Y)^2+(AB+CD)^2>2(AC^2+BC^2+AD^2+BD^2)+2Y(BC+AD).$$

**Step 2.** Expand: $(X+Y)^2+(AB+CD)^2-2Y(BC+AD)=X^2+Y^2+2Y(X-BC-AD)+(AB+CD)^2=X^2+Y^2+2Y(AB+CD)+(AB+CD)^2=X^2+Z^2$. So it suffices to show $X^2+Z^2>2(AC^2+BC^2+AD^2+BD^2)$, i.e. (doubling)
$$[X^2-4BD^2]+[X^2-4AC^2]+[Z^2-4BC^2]+[Z^2-4AD^2]>0.$$

**Step 3.** Each bracket is positive by the triangle inequality: $X>2BD$ because $BC+CD>BD$ and $DA+AB>BD$; $X>2AC$ because $AB+BC>AC$ and $CD+DA>AC$; $Z>2BC$ because $AB+AC>BC$ and $CD+BD>BC$; $Z>2AD$ because $AB+BD>AD$ and $AC+CD>AD$. All steps are reversible inequalities in the right direction, so the original inequality holds. $\blacksquare$
